winner.title: Soup Joumou (Haitian Squash Soup)

evidence.authenticity: Traditional structure: epis marinade for chuck, calabaza squash puree, turnips, carrots, potatoes, cabbage, pasta, whole habanero (Scotch bonnet stand-in). Adaptations: chicken broth, rigatoni, cloves in a cheesecloth bundle. Author is not Haitian, but ATK also has a companion article 'How to Make Soup Joumou'. Headnote frames it as Haiti's New Year's ritual.
evidence.precision: Weights/sizes for 5 ingredients; vegetables cut to stated sizes (1.5-inch, 1-inch); 15 sensory/doneness cues (beef fork-tender with 2 cups liquid remaining, squash tender but not falling apart 12-15 min, root veg just shy of tender, pasta rests covered 4-6 min); Dutch oven named but no inch/quart size; no temperatures.
evidence.testing: ATK test kitchen recipe. Make-ahead notes for epis and puree, and the pasta is finished off heat to avoid mush. Rating 3.8 from only 18 ratings. Detailed 'why' text is behind the login.
evidence.photos: Step images not in schema (stepImagesInSchema 0, 19 images on page). Judged from ATK's usual practice, which is hidden behind login; not marked down heavily.
evidence.efficiency: Epis and squash puree are made while beef marinates. 3h45m total is realistic. Making a double batch of epis and boiling squash separately adds a few steps.
evidence.access: Calabaza is the hard item (found at Latino or Caribbean markets); kabocha or butternut works as a sub, though the page text read did not state it. Habanero replaces Scotch bonnet. Everything else is at a normal grocery.

winner.why: Beat the NYT version on precision and tested-recipe rigor: it gives explicit doneness cues for beef, squash, vegetables and pasta, where NYT mostly gives times.

runnerUp.title: Soup Joumou
runnerUp.source: NYT Cooking (Priya Krishna, with Cindy Similien)

evidence.authenticity: Developed with Haitian chef Cindy Similien. Includes epis, lime-washed beef, calabaza puree, Scotch bonnet left whole, vermicelli and hand-rolled dumplings (a traditional element). Headnote explains the independence story.
evidence.precision: Only 2 ingredients with weights; produce sized (medium, large); 4 sensory cues; no temperatures; no pot size ('large pot'); several steps are time-only.
evidence.testing: NYT Cooking, 395 ratings at 4 stars. Notes on bursting the pepper and thinning the soup, but little reasoning.
evidence.photos: No step images in schema (45 images on page, likely mostly unrelated).
evidence.efficiency: 2 hours plus marination; dumplings made while soup cooks. Includes a full epis recipe.
evidence.access: Calabaza and Scotch bonnet needed; no subs stated in the schema.

runnerUp.why: Slightly more authentic (dumplings, Haitian co-author) but less precise on doneness.

candidates.disqualified: No steps in the recipe; adds coconut milk and corn, so it is an adaptation
Page is a magazine story with no ingredient amounts
Loaded (200) but no structured data; not scored

soup joumou soup au giraumon recette haïtienne
notes: Scores of ATK and NYT are close (73 vs 69); NYT is the better pick if you want a Haitian co-author, dumplings and 395 ratings. Saveur's Elle Philippe (grew up in Port-au-Prince) is the most authoritative voice but has no process photos or pan sizes, and gets 58. Calabaza is the main US access issue; kabocha or butternut is the usual sub. The Save the Children page was not scored, because I did not read its ingredients or steps.
